activities.anchor: Governance's first principle is that people follow their incentives
activities.caption: pair each failure mode with its corrective tool
activities.name: govToolMatch

config.prompt: Incentive design is control — pair each failure with the tool that guards it:

pairs.left: results later proven false were already paid

config.why: Equity pay aligns managers with owners only directionally — share-price movements can be manufactured by buybacks and cost-cutting as easily as by value creation.

config.root: You run a firm generating cash well beyond good investment opportunities. Jensen (1986) is watching — and so are the owners.

start.text: The cash pile grows. What does the firm do with it?

choices.label: Expand — acquisitions, prestige projects, headcount
choices.feedback: The empire is the manager's utility and the payout is only the shareholder's — the classic drift the hypothesis names.

choices.label: Return it — dividends and buybacks
choices.feedback: Contracted cash exits: the disciplining answer, because the money can no longer fund pet projects.

empire.text: The owners notice the returns on the expansions are thin. What arrives next?

choices.label: Debt — which contracts future discretion
choices.feedback: Governance in miniature: interest payments commit the cash before managers can spend it.

choices.label: A takeover bid
choices.feedback: The threat of takeover is the market's attempt to take the discretionary money back — the LBO wave followed exactly this logic in the cash-rich oil industry of the early 1980s.

return.text: Discretionary money exits under contract — the empire-builder's budget is gone.

debt.text: Future discretion contracted away: discipline without a bid.

takeover.text: New owners, new management — the external corrector for appointment failure.

config.why: Jensen's own target was the oil industry of the early 1980s — cash-rich firms drilling anyway — and the leveraged-buyout wave was the market's answer.

activities.anchor: A board that starts managing operations has usually already failed at its actual jobs
activities.caption: true or false — oversight versus running
activities.name: govBoardJudge

statements.s: The board runs the company's operations.
The board's actual jobs include hiring and firing the CEO, approving strategy and major transactions, and overseeing risk and audit.
statements.why: Those three jobs require information and courage, not meeting time.

statements.s: A board that starts managing operations has usually already abandoned overseeing.
statements.why: Running operations is the failure signature, not a sign of engagement.

statements.s: A weak board is decoration with liability.
statements.why: The machinery only works when the people in it are willing to say no.

activities.caption: file each duty under its committee
activities.name: govCommitteeBuckets

config.prompt: One-tier boards work through committees. File each duty:

items.label: financial integrity and the external auditor relationship

config.why: Each committee carries independence requirements the codes specify — and CEO/chair separation plus genuinely independent audit committees correlate with fewer restatements.

activities.anchor: Britain's Corporate Governance Code runs on
activities.caption: drag the divider — two theories of who enforces
activities.name: govCodeCompare

config.prompt: Enforcement philosophies — drag the divider across the systems:

before.label: UK — comply or explain
before.text: Listing rules with principles that companies may depart from if they explain why to the market — a bet that investor scrutiny beats prescription.

after.label: US — legislated duties
after.text: Sarbanes–Oxley and exchange listing standards legislate specific duties, with regulators and criminal liability behind them.

config.why: None is clearly superior in outcomes; Germany's statutory two-tier removes some choices entirely — and cross-listed firms must satisfy all three national theories of who enforces governance.

activities.anchor: together hold on the order of a fifth
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the index managers' votes
activities.name: govIndexEstimate

config.prompt: BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street together hold roughly what fraction of a typical S&P 500 company's votes?
config.why: About a fifth — engagement runs through proxy voting: directors elected, auditors appointed, and since Dodd-Frank (2010) an advisory say-on-pay vote.
config.context: The open tension: passive funds cannot sell without un-indexing, so their governance power is decoupled from their economic exposure.

activities.anchor: an advisory vote produces information, a binding one produces bargaining
activities.caption: one line of the say-on-pay summary is reversed
activities.name: govSayPaySpot

config.prompt: One line of this say-on-pay summary has the mechanism design backwards. Find it.
lines: The US say-on-pay vote (Dodd-Frank, 2010) is advisory
Britain escalated to a binding statutory vote on remuneration policy from October 2013
A UK pay policy needs shareholder approval to operate at all
An advisory vote produces bargaining; a binding one produces information
Boards now negotiate pay packages with proxy advisers before the meeting
config.correction: An advisory vote produces information; a binding one produces bargaining.
config.why: The regimes differ in legal force — and that difference, not the word 'vote', is what changes how boards behave before the meeting.

activities.anchor: Whistleblowing channels belong in the same system
activities.caption: fill the blanks — appointment is destiny
activities.name: govAppointCloze

config.text: Governance failures are usually %%0%% failures with a time lag: the wrong CEO selected, the compliant director retained, the auditor chosen for friendliness. Directors who owe their seats to the CEO are structurally compromised — the '%%1%% director' problem. Whistleblowing channels are the recruitment of %%2%%.
